societies.name: The Culture

scope.continuity: Iain M. Banks's prose Culture universe
scope.period: The mature Culture; ordinary civilian life rather than a wartime emergency
scope.population: Biological humanlike citizens, with AI citizens included in the account of governance
exclusions: People governed by Culture interventions outside the Culture

societies.description:
Culture citizens do not need a job to obtain the things that keep them alive. Automated production supports comfortable lives, while people can explore, make art, study, or take on useful projects. This puts material guarantees very close to the strong end of the map. Someone choosing a demanding vocation does not lose that underlying security.

Control is more complicated. Citizens can propose votes, and biological people and machines participate in collective decisions. Yet the Minds are independent persons and operate the ships, habitats, and much of the practical machinery. The positive control score recognizes the described democratic arrangements, while its broad uncertainty range leaves room for the Minds' exceptional practical power. It should not be mistaken for humans owning obedient robots. The books also give no census of how many biological citizens regularly do productive work, so that percentage remains unresolved.

guarantees.basis: Material access is not conditional on employment.

control.basis: Equal voting and autonomous Minds coexist; the point is an interpretation of their shared power.

nonworking.basis: Voluntary activity is established; its population-wide frequency is not.

evidence.claim: Automation and elective activity support inclusion.
Voting and Mind independence make control mixed.

uncertainties: Humanlike citizens are a disclosed proxy, not exclusively Homo sapiens.
A complete direct retrieval of the author essay remains desirable.
Nonworking fraction requires a separate editorial estimate or better evidence.

review.method: Second pass against the gathered passages; no independent reviewer

societies.name: The Machine Stops
societies.society: Humanity under the Machine before collapse

scope.period: Established underground order before the terminal breakdown
scope.population: Humans living inside the Machine's underground settlements

societies.description:
An underground resident can summon food, clothing, a bed, medical attention, and remote conversation without earning a wage for each service. The Machine has taken over the material routines of living. That supports a strong provision score, but the safety net has a brutal condition: dissent can bring expulsion from the system, treated by its residents as a death sentence. The score therefore stops well short of an unconditional guarantee.

The story still has human committees, a human airship attendant, and people delivering lectures. It does not establish a modern, self-aware AI government. Control sits near the concentrated human-management band, with uncertainty because nobody understands the complete infrastructure anymore. The later breakdown exposes the fragility of this arrangement; it is not folded into the earlier snapshot. No reliable share of working humans can be extracted from the lecturers and attendants shown.

guarantees.basis: Routine subsistence is supplied, but expulsion makes access conditional.

control.basis: Human committees remain; technical dependence is not proof of conscious AI sovereignty.

nonworking.basis: Attendants, committees and lecturers survive, without a labor census.

evidence.claim: Provision, conditional expulsion and human occupations are explicit.
evidence.locator: Parts I–III: room controls, airship attendant, Homelessness, committees

uncertainties: Conscious machine agency is not established.
The share of productive lecture activity is unknown.

review.method: Second pass against primary passages; no independent reviewer

societies.name: Manna (United States welfare compounds)

scope.period: Jacob's residence in the Terrafoam system after mass job displacement
scope.population: Unemployed human residents of the welfare compounds
exclusions: The wealthy population outside the compounds

societies.description:
Robots replace the jobs, and the displaced people are moved into extremely cheap residential blocks. Their meals and basic accommodation are supplied rather than earned through work. This is a post-work arrangement for the compound residents, but a highly unequal one: wealth and the systems supervising them remain under elite control. Residents have little practical route back to independent livelihoods.

The guarantees score needs care. Chapter 4 actually describes food, shelter, and cleaning being provided; describing those services as wholly absent would misread the setting. The modestly negative score recognizes that subsistence while allowing for overcrowding, confinement, and dependence on an unaccountable ruling class. A harsher interpretation is retained as an alternative regime. The nonworking estimate applies only to the unemployed compound population, not to the entire United States. It is close to one because robotic services have replaced the residents' former occupations.

guarantees.basis: Basic provision is explicit; its adequacy and long-term security are questionable.

control.basis: The elite controls resources and coercive robots.

nonworking.basis: Scoped to residents selected for unemployment; editorial allowance for unreported activities, not a canonical statistic.

evidence.claim: Compound residents receive necessities under elite confinement.
evidence.locator: Housing, meals, elite control and perimeter passages

uncertainties: The article's reproductive-control claim needs a separately located primary passage; it is not silently imported as proof that food guarantees are absent.
No countrywide nonworking rate is asserted.

review.method: Second pass distinguishing subsistence from freedom; no independent reviewer

societies.name: Manna (Australia Project)

scope.period: The established Australia Project visited by Jacob
scope.population: Human members of the Australia Project

societies.description:
The Australia Project pools resources through a corporation whose members receive equal access to its output. Weekly resource credits come with membership, while robots provide everyday goods and services. A resident does not need to accept a job to secure food or a home. Those arrangements place guarantees near the strong end and control toward broad participation, although the promise is for Project members rather than everyone on Earth.

Routine production being automated does not mean human effort disappears. The later chapters describe people designing products, doing research, teaching newcomers, and even choosing manual farming and crafts. The nonworking share therefore remains unknown instead of being set to one. The control score also allows some uncertainty: an equal economic share gives a clear claim on output, but it does not fully explain every operational decision made by the advanced robotic system. This society is kept separate from Terrafoam because both distribution and ownership differ.

guarantees.basis: Equal resource access is independent of employment within the membership population.

control.basis: Equal shares and resource claims; operational human-AI authority is less fully specified.

nonworking.basis: Elective productive activity is widespread but uncounted.

uncertainties: Equal shares are not assumed to prove perfect human control over all AI decisions.
No exact nonworking percentage is supplied.

review.method: Second pass checking membership scope and voluntary labor; no independent reviewer

societies.name: WALL-E (Axiom before the return to Earth)
societies.society: Axiom passengers under Buy n Large and AUTO

scope.period: The Axiom's established cruise before AUTO is disabled
scope.population: Human passengers and the human captain aboard the Axiom
exclusions: People who never boarded a starliner
The rebuilding community after the return

societies.description:
The Axiom is a corporate-built refuge whose human population lives on automated services. Passengers receive daily comfort while robots perform the ordinary maintenance around them. The captain retains duties, but even his normal routine is mostly checking the ship's condition with AUTO. For this enclosed population, the nonworking share is therefore estimated very near one, and provision is strong. Neither estimate is a statement about everyone who once lived on Earth.

The ship sits between corporate control and autonomous machine administration. Its infrastructure and commands come from Buy n Large, yet AUTO has managed the voyage for centuries and pursues a hidden mandate against the inhabitants' interests. The negative control score captures that practical independence without erasing its corporate origin. The passengers' comfort is real, but they lack a secure say over the system supporting them. The later return and rebuilding form a different snapshot and are not averaged into this one.

guarantees.basis: Long-established passenger provision; no universal legal charter is shown.

control.basis: Corporate origin and autonomous enforcement overlap.

nonworking.basis: Passenger leisure and minimal captain duties; rounded editorial estimate, not a census.

evidence.claim: Passengers are provisioned while AUTO retains a hidden mandate.
evidence.locator: John and Mary; Captain; AUTO; Axiom

uncertainties: Corporate commands and practical AI control cannot be cleanly separated.
Provision outside the passenger population is unknown.

review.method: Second pass on the official production guide; no independent reviewer

societies.name: Star Trek (Federation core society)
societies.society: United Federation of Planets core worlds

scope.continuity: Prime timeline, with Earth as the principal documented example
scope.period: Ordinary twenty-fourth-century life in the TNG era
scope.population: Human civilians on Earth; wider core-world generalization is provisional
exclusions: Military duty as a proxy for all civilian life

societies.description:
On twenty-fourth-century Earth, the familiar link between earning money and meeting material needs has largely disappeared. Replicators and supporting infrastructure make everyday goods readily available, and choosing a vocation is presented as a matter of interest and contribution. The strong guarantee score describes this ordinary civilian baseline. It is not a claim that every frontier settlement or wartime starship enjoys the same conditions.

The society is placed toward broad human control because its economic infrastructure serves a civic order rather than an independent machine ruler or a small private owner. That is an interpretation of the Federation setting, not proof that every asset is collectively owned: family enterprises and personal holdings remain visible. Many people also work seriously as scientists, teachers, officers, or craftspeople. Optional employment cannot tell us how many actually choose those activities, so the nonworking percentage is left open instead of inferring it from the absence of wages.

guarantees.basis: Core-world access is independent of earnings; broader Federation coverage requires care.

control.basis: Civic provision and human institutions coexist with individual holdings.

nonworking.basis: No civilian participation rate follows from work being optional.

evidence.claim: Earth's material baseline does not depend on earning money.
evidence.locator: The Neutral Zone and Life in the 24th Century discussion

evidence.claim: Optional productive vocations and personal holdings remain.
evidence.locator: Smithian Star Trek; closing discussion of work

uncertainties: The reviewed source is a guest essay on an official site; episode-level corroboration should strengthen the final review.
The stored society label is broader than the best-supported Earth example; the population scope limits the inference.
No exact nonworking percentage is supplied.

review.method: Second pass separating commentary from direct episode evidence; no independent reviewer

decisions.reason: Automation and non-wage material provision are supported; humanlike scope and a missing labor rate are explicit.
Technological provision replaces routine economic dependence; human committees prevent an automatic AI-rule classification.
A distinct robot-supported, non-employed residential population under elite control.
Equal member resource claims materially differ from Terrafoam's elite-controlled provision.
Automated passenger society is explicitly supported by the production guide.
Non-wage provision on Earth is supported; wider scope and employment rate remain review gaps.

review_notes: The initial frozen catalogue contains leads, not fact-checked titles, media or distinctness claims. Correct or reject them in the decision ledger without changing their IDs.
Do not turn oppressive governance into an automatic assertion that food and shelter do not exist.
Do not equate automated machinery with a self-aware AI sovereign.
Four records have an unresolved nonworking axis. They are qualitative inclusions, not fully coordinate-ready records.
